title: Watermelon
wiki_lead:
The watermelon (Citrullus lanatus) is a species of flowering plant in the family Cucurbitaceae. It is a scrambling and trailing vine-like plant cultivated worldwide for its fruit, a large berry with a firm rind and no internal divisions, botanically termed a pepo. The sweet, juicy flesh is usually deep red to pink, with many seeds that are black when mature and white when immature.
The modern watermelon originated in Sudan, where it was first domesticated and cultivated. Kordofan melons are the closest relatives, and may be progenitors of modern, cultivated watermelons. Watermelons were domesticated in Sudan and cultivated in Egypt by 2000 BCE. Dessert watermelons spread around the Mediterranean world during Roman antiquity. Considerable breeding effort has developed disease-resistant and seedless varieties. Many cultivars are available that produce mature fruit within 100 days of planting. In 2024, China produced 60% of the world's watermelons.
Watermelons are grown in tropical to temperate regions for its fruit, which can be eaten raw or used to make juice or wine. The rind is also edible after being pickled or cooked.

Description
The watermelon is an annual plant that has a prostrate or climbing habit, spreading out up to 2 metres (7 feet). The leaves are alternate, lobed (sometimes with serrated margins), 6 to 20 centimetres (2+1⁄2 to 8 inches) long, and 4 to 15 cm (1+1⁄2 to 6 in) wide. Young growth is densely woolly with yellowish-brown hairs which disappear as the plant ages. It has branching tendrils.
The species is monoecious, with male and female flowers produced on the same plant. Blooming from July to August, the five-petaled flowers are white or yellow and borne on 40-millimetre-long (1+1⁄2 in) hairy stalks. Each flower grows singly in the leaf axils, with five petals fused into a cup. The male flowers predominate at the beginning of the season; the female flowers, which develop later, have inferior ovaries. The styles are united into a single column.
The large fruit is a kind of modified berry called a pepo, with a thick rind and fleshy center (mesocarp and endocarp). Wild plants have fruits up to 20 cm (8 in) in diameter, while cultivated varieties may exceed 60 cm (24 in). The rind of the fruit is mid- to dark green and usually mottled or striped, and the flesh, containing numerous seeds spread throughout the inside, can be red or pink (most commonly), orange, yellow, green or white.
A bitter watermelon, C. amarus, has become naturalized in semiarid regions of several continents, and is designated as a "pest plant" in parts of Western Australia, where they are called "pig melons".


Taxonomy
The sweet watermelon was first described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753 and given the name Cucurbita citrullus. It was reassigned to the genus Citrullus in 1836, under the replacement name Citrullus vulgaris, by the German botanist Heinrich Adolf Schrader. (The International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants does not allow names like "Citrullus citrullus".)
The species is further divided into several varieties, of which bitter wooly melon (Citrullus lanatus [Thunb.] Matsum. & Nakai var. lanatus), citron melons (Citrullus lanatus var. citroides [L. H. Bailey] Mansf.), and the edible var. vulgaris are common. This taxonomy originated with the erroneous synonymization of the wooly melon Citrullus lanatus with the sweet watermelon Citrullus vulgaris by L. H. Bailey in 1930. Molecular data, including sequences from the original collection of Thunberg and other relevant type material, show that the sweet watermelon (Citrullus vulgaris Schrad.) and the bitter wooly melon Citrullus lanatus (Thunb.) Matsum. & Nakai are not closely related to each other. A proposal to conserve the name, Citrullus lanatus (Thunb.) Matsum. & Nakai, was accepted by the nomenclature committee and confirmed at the International Botanical Congress in 2017.

grok_lead: The watermelon ( Citrullus lanatus) is a species of annual flowering plant in the Cucurbitaceae family, characterized by trailing vines that produce large, oblong to spherical fruits with a tough rind enclosing juicy, edible flesh typically red or pink in color and containing numerous seeds. The fruit consists primarily of water (about 92% by weight), making it low in calories at approximately 46 per cup of diced flesh, while providing modest amounts of vitamins A and C, potassium, and the amino acid citrulline. Native to Africa, where wild ancestors were valued for their water content in arid environments, the plant's domestication traces back over 5,000 years, with archaeological seeds recovered from Neolithic sites in Libya and depictions alongside offerings in ancient Egyptian tombs dating to around 2000 BCE. Today, watermelons are cultivated worldwide in warm climates, yielding fruits that range from small personal sizes to record-breaking specimens exceeding 100 kilograms, with selective breeding yielding seedless varieties and diverse flesh colors including yellow.
